newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran appoints first woman mayor, prosecutor.
newsitem.headline: Iran appoints first woman mayor, prosecutor.

text.p: Iranian authorities have appointed a women as a mayor and another as an assistant prosecutor for the first time since the 1979 Islamic revolution, newspapers said on Monday.

The daily Hamshahri said Zahra Sadrazam Nouri, former head of a cultural centre in southern Tehran and a teachers' college lecturer, was named by Tehran mayor Gholamhossein Karbaschi as mayor of one of the capital's 20 districts.
A female assistant prosecutor has also been appointed, judiciary head Ayatollah Mohammad Yazdi told the daily Iran. He said she would soon start work but did not name her.
Tehran has rejected repeated criticism by the United Nations Human Rights Commission and other monitoring bodies that it discriminated against women and violated their rights.
Iran's highest female official is Shahla Habibi, President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani's adviser on women's affairs.
Yazdi said several women worked as legal advisers in family courts and a woman was deputy head of the justice ministry's local administration in Tehran.
"Of course ladies working in the judiciary cannot head a court and issue rulings as a judge," Yazdi said, referring to Iran's Islamic rules which do not allow women to become judges.
Some local women's publications have questioned the rules and supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei earlier this month appeared to be calling for more debate on the issue.

"Such debates are excellent and appropriate, and Islamic principles on such issues as employing women as judges or other posts should be studied and discussed," Khamenei was quoted by state-run Tehran radio as saying.
"There has been a lot of debate on women's issues, but only small steps have been taken and there is much work to be done," he said, stressing however that Iran should not "copy the West".

Khamenei and other senior Iranian clerics have blasted the Taleban Islamic militia in neighbouring Afghanistan as "un-Islamic" and said it gave Islam a bad name by stopping women from working out of homes and girls from attending schools.
Iran's highest woman official before the revolution, a minister of education, was executed in 1979 after being convicted by an Islamic revolutionary court on morals and corruption charges.
